keyframes.prompt: Vertical 2:3 macro nature photo at ground level, side view. Damp dark brown garden soil fills the lower half of the frame, with a few small green grass sprouts and one dry brown leaf in the soft out-of-focus background. In the center of the frame, in a small shallow hollow in the soil, lies a small group of about twenty cricket eggs: each egg is cream-yellow, smooth, slightly curved like a tiny banana, about one twenty-fifth of the frame width long. Soft daylight, sharp focus on the eggs. Keep everything important away from the left and right edges. No text, no watermark.

Edit this image. Keep the soil, the hollow, the grass, the leaf, background, lighting and camera angle exactly the same. The eggs are hatching: many tiny newly hatched cricket nymphs crawl out of the eggs onto the soil. Each nymph is pale white, wingless, with long thin antennae and long hind legs, about one twentieth of the frame width long. Some egg shells are now empty and split open. No text, no watermark.

Edit this image. Keep the soil, the hollow with the empty split egg shells, the grass, the leaf, background, lighting and camera angle exactly the same. The group of white nymphs is gone. One small cricket nymph now stands on the soil just in front of the empty egg shells, in the center of the frame, seen from the side, head facing left. It is dark brown-black with a thin white band across its back, wingless, with long antennae, about one eighth of the frame width long. Only one cricket. No text, no watermark.

Edit this image. Keep the soil, the empty egg shells, the grass, the leaf, background, lighting and camera angle exactly the same. The nymph in the same place and pose is now much bigger: a large black-brown cricket nymph with small wing buds on its back and a short spike at the tip of its abdomen, about one quarter of the frame width long. Its pale old shed skin lies on the soil just behind it. Only one cricket. No text, no watermark.

Edit this image. Keep the soil, the empty egg shells, the shed skin, the grass, the leaf, background, lighting and camera angle exactly the same. The large nymph is now an adult female two-spotted field cricket in the same place and pose: glossy black body, two small pale yellow spots at the base of its wings, dark wings folded flat over its back, very long antennae, and a long thin straight needle-like ovipositor at the rear, about two fifths of the frame width long. A second pale shed skin lies on the soil behind it. Only one cricket. No text, no watermark.

Edit this image. Keep the soil, the old empty egg shells, the shed skins, the grass, the leaf, background, lighting and camera angle exactly the same. The same adult female cricket, with the same size and colors, stands in the same place, its abdomen slightly bent down, and pushes the tip of its long ovipositor down into the soil. A few new cream-yellow eggs lie half buried in the soil next to the ovipositor tip. Only one cricket. No text, no watermark.
